Hi Scott,

You should convert the results to a data.frame first, and then export the data.frame using write.csv() or a similar function. See the example at the end the help page for modSel():

ms <- modSel(fl, nullmod="Null")
ms

coef(ms)                            # Estimates only
SE(ms)                              # Standard errors only
(toExport <- as(ms, "data.frame"))  # Everything

Richard

Hello,

Thanks in advance from any help. I have read multiple relevant posts on here, but still not solved my error.
Please note data is attached.

I can create an unmarked frame for pcountOpen using the below code:

# Load data
cnt <- read.csv("count_dat_wide_format_igm_iga_analysis.csv", header = TRUE)
siteCovs <- read.csv("siteCovs_igm_iga_analysis.csv", header = TRUE)
yearlySiteCovs <- read.csv("yearlySiteCovs2_igm_iga_analysis.csv", header = TRUE)

# Create UMF
umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y = cnt, siteCovs = siteCovs, yearlySiteCovs = yearlySiteCovs, numPrimary = 29)

However, when I run:

I have not been able to work out why I get this error. I note that the the unmarkedFramePCO() help file suggests that yearlySiteCovs can be a list of MxJ dataframes, but I have clearly coded something incorrectly.
Any help would be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Error in pcountOpen or unmarkedFramePCO
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Error in pcountOpen or unmarkedFramePCO
messages.body_plain:
Hello Pat,

Your data loads okay and calling "summary(umf)" shows it has created the unmarkedFrame Object - review these values to ensure your data appear correct.

The issue is your formula. See the R Documentation for pcountOpen for full descriptions of pcountOpen and unmarkedFramePCO.

The first argument for lambda is for initial abundance and takes a single-season, "Site-level covariates". In your case siteCovs: state,site. The three variables you have provided are multi-year "Yearly-site-level covariates", hence the error that a list was provided when it is expecting a single variable.

The second and third arguments are for gamma and omega which will take the "yearly-site-level covariates" - in your case the yearlySiteCovs: year, season, distance.

The fourth is for detection probability. For this you will need observation-level covariates for each value of y, of which you have not provided any.

You may have trouble fitting lambda (initial abundance) with samples from only one site in the first season.  Without knowing your plans or requirements, you may have to truncate the data to start in ~2015 when you have more sites surveyed. Alternatively, if you only want abundance estimates for each site in each season (without modelling gamma or omega) you may get results by stacking your data into a single season and using pcount (although this treats each site*season as independent, which may not be appealing).

Of course, I'm happy to be corrected on any/all of this.

Cheers,
Alistair

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrienne,

This warning...

>
> 3: In gdistsamp(~site + roughness + elevation + closed.D + total.BA +  :
>   Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates and supplying starting values.
>

...indicates why standard errors are missing (SE is derived from Var-Covar Matrix which is derived from Hessian) and gives some suggestions. There should be a bunch of threads here asking about 'Hessian is singular' that will contain some further suggestions--often, it can be easier to fit models with many parameters by slowing stepping up (e.g., fit a model with a few parameters, concatenate these estimates and some zeroes to provide starting values for a model with more parameters).  Detection and hazard rate look a little funky to me, so that might be a place to start.

Re. K, fitting the model using MLE requires integrating the latent site-specific abundance N_i out of the likelihood (roughly, summing N_i|lambda_i and y_i|N_i across N_i = 0, 1, 2, ...K ). K denotes this upper limit. If it is too small, the parameter estimates are going to be biased, and as it increases, the model will take longer to fit because there are more calculations going on. My understanding is that the general rule of thumb is that a reasonable value for K is one where, if you increase it (say from K=50 to K=51 or K=60), the estimates do not change.

Sometimes with an NB mixture, estimates do not stabilize at any value for K, which indicates the model is not identifiable, although I don't know that I've heard of this being a problem for distance sampling models.

Anyway, hopefully this explanation is approximately correct enough to move forward with.

Cheers,

John

messages.body_plain:
The P>|z| values have no meaning for intercept terms--this is a Wald test for whether the parameter value is different than 0.

Maybe try the link below for the warning message--it's a pretty common one. Really, I think the best way to go about this is to start with fitting simpler models and then build up. I might start with a model that looks like:

m1<-gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~slope.A + elevation + closed.D +
    total.BA + shannon, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~1, data = g.umf,
    keyfun = "hazard", output = "density", unitsOut = "kmsq",
    mixture = c("NB"), K = 50, se = TRUE)

Maybe (or maybe not), providing the starting values based upon this model would allow this:

m2<-gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~slope.A + elevation + closed.D +
    total.BA + shannon+site, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~1, data = g.umf,
    keyfun = "hazard", output = "density", unitsOut = "kmsq",
    mixture = c("NB"), K = 50, se = TRUE, starts=c(coef(m1)[1:6], rep(0, 11), coef(m1)[7:9]))

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Thanks in advance for any help.

I have counts of animals on three consecutive nights, at four time points throughout the year (summer, autumn, winter, spring), across seven years. However, my aim is purely to predict abundance at each combination of site*season*year and so I have chosen to use pcount() instead of pcountOpen() as I have no interest in modelling gamma or omega.

I can create my data frame with no problems, but when I run and then summarise my desired model I get warning: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj))) : NaNs produced, and have NANs in my model output. There are several good posts on this group that describe similar problems (here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/In$20sqrt(diag(vcov(obj)))$20$3A$20NaNs$20produced$20pcount%7Csort:date/unmarked/7yxaws9gW4E/GwztkwPl348J> and here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/In$20sqrt(diag(vcov(obj)))$20$3A$20NaNs$20produced$20pcount%7Csort:date/unmarked/HNRjDiDA-Ws/Rp53sCMNEAAJ>), but these have not yet helped me to solve my error.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Please see data attached and code below.

# Load data
pcnt <- read.csv("pcount_dat.csv", header = TRUE)

# Define y and siteCovs
y <- pcnt[,2:4]
siteCovs <- pcnt[,6:9]

# Create UMF
umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = y, siteCovs = siteCovs)
summary(umf)

# Run model
m2 <- pcount(~site ~site + year + season + offset(log(dist)), data = umf, K = 574, mixture = "NB", se = TRUE)
summary(m2)

# Once I am confident my model works appropriately, I plan to predict from this model as follows
new_dat <- siteCovs
new_dat$dist <- 1

pred <- predict(m2, type = "state", newdata = new_dat)
pred$abun <- exp(pred$Predicted)

messages.body_plain:
A quick fix is to subtract 2000 from year.  (4-digit years cause a lot of issues in all types if iterative fitting procedures especially if a squared year is used.)  So an additional line of code right after

> siteCovs <- pcnt[,6:9]

might be

> siteCovs$year <- siteCovs$year - 2000

Then there are no NaN's.

So this is essentially related to "standardizing" covariates.  For things like 4-digit years subtracting 2000 (or 1900 or 1990 if you're analyzing older data) is easier to do (and undo) and easier to interpret than subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.

Probably too much or unnecessary information:  The Hessian when using 4-digit years has two negative entries and when the inverse of that matrix is taken negative values appear along the diagonal where the estimates of variance are taken.  Taking the square root of those negative numbers results in R showing NaN's for those standard errors.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: Combining distance and time removal methods?
messages.subject_clean: Combining distance and time removal methods?
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I'm wondering if there are any updates to unmarked that would relate to this topic.  I have a dataset very similar to what Courtney describes here (i.e., distance data with time-to-detection recorded in intervals).  So, I'm wanting to use the distance data with the time data to estimate both availability and detectability (and ultimately model density with a number of survey- and site-specific covariates).  I'm trying to figure out the best approach for analyzing these data.  I have a general sense, but . . . I'm not entirely sure how to code for time-to-detection.  Any sample code out there?

Thanks,

Jason

On Monday, July 9, 2012 at 8:13:58 PM UTC+1, camundson wrote:
> Hi-
>
> I wanted to run this by the group just to make sure I'm not missing something.
>
> I have single-visit point count data where observers estimated time to detection and distance.  In order to account for both availability and detection to estimate density (e.g., Farnsworth et al. 2005), I 'd like to combine the two methods - which isn't a currently available combo in unmarked - I don't believe.
>
> So, to get at that, I could use a 2-staged process by first running a removal-type analysis (multinomPois) and then using those predicted counts to input into a distance analysis (distsamp)?  I would then include covariates on abundance into the second analysis and use those estimates of density (the ultimate objective).  Does that sound appropriate?
>
> Thanks!
>
> Courtney

messages.body_plain:
Hi Krisztina,

Formulas in r (almost always or always incorporating the tilde in some fashion --e.g., y~x, y~1, etc.) are objects that help the fitting machinery find the necessary variables, set up the model matrix, and so forth. pcountOpen is no different in this regard: the first three arguments are formulas for models of initial abundance, recruitment, survival, etc., and so this is where one would specify a model for the variation in initial abundance/recruitment/survival with covariates and/or interactions/polynomials/other transformations. I think the only 'numbers' you need to provide unmarked are self contained in the unmarked frame (the detections in whatever form, distance bands for certain models, maybe something I'm forgetting). The formulas are looking for the same sort of compact description of the model structure regardless of the argument for 'dynamics', but maybe worth re-iterating the documentation in noting that the interpretation of the parameters changes depending upon how dynamics are specified.

John

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I'm having trouble finding any information about this error in the group or anywhere else, and haven't been able to fix it on my own.
I have created and run my global model in gdistsamp and would now like to run a GOF test with bootstrap iterations to determine model fit.
I ran fitstats, which seems to work fine, but then when I run the bootstrap function I get an error about an "invalid second argument 'size'".
Any thoughts??

> fitstats <- function(g.global) {
+   observed <- getY(g.global@data)
+   expected <- fitted(g.global)
+   resids <- residuals(g.global)
+   sse <- sum(resids^2, na.rm = TRUE)
+   chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected, na.rm = TRUE)
+   freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2, na.rm = TRUE)
+   out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
+   return(out)
+ }

> (g.pb <- parboot(g.global, fitstats, nsim=10, report=5))

t0 = 97959.52 3578.87 2954.002
Error in rmultinom(1, N, prob = cp.it <http://cp.it>) : invalid second argument 'size'
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In rnbinom(1, mu = lambda[i], size = alpha) : NAs produced
2: In rbinom(1, Ns, phi[i, t]) : NAs produced

messages.body_plain:
Dear Adrienne,

the cheapest means of dealing with missing covariate values in your situation is to simply replace the missings with the mean of the covariate values measured at the other sites. There are more elegant, and more correct ways of dealing with missing covariates, but they are all much more complicated in a sense, and since you only have a very small proportion of sites with missing covariates, doing this cheap solution will hardly affect anything.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: predict () detection across season
messages.body_plain:
I am struggling to set up a newdata dataframe for use in the predict () function. My goal is to predict how detection probably changes over the season. A season is the time between the min and max dates. Here is my N-mixture model:

m.age2 = pcount(~YR + date_s + LCR_s    ~ poly(Age_s,2, raw=TRUE), data=umf)

where YR is a factor (2 levels, 2018 and 2019, we surveyed 151 sites in 2018 and 158 different sites in 2019) and
date_s (Julian), LCR_s, and Age_s are all continuous.

date_s is an observation covariate and has 3 survey dates per site over the season. My code follows. At the end, it is incomplete because I haven't figured out how to get date_s into the newdata dataframe. My confusion stems from the fact that all the other covariates are site level covariates and therefore only have one value per site, while date_s has 3 values per site. Thank you in advance for any suggestions.
Scott

# observations
C = cbind(SPP$Observed_1, SPP$Observed_2, SPP$Observed_3)

#site covariates
Age = SPP[, "Age"]
LCR = SPP[,"mLCR"]
YR = as.factor(SPP[, "surv_yresh"])

#Observation covariates
date = cbind(SPP$YDAY_1, SPP$YDAY_2, SPP$YDAY_3)

umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(
         y = C,
         siteCovs = data.frame(Age_s = scale(Age),
                               LCR_s = scale(LCR),
                               YR),
         obsCovs = list(date_s = scale(date),
                        time_s = scale(time),
                        observer = observer)  )
summary(umf)

# detection by date
m.age2 = pcount(~YR + date_s + LCR_s    ~ poly(Age_s,2, raw=TRUE), data=umf)
newdat = data.frame(Age_s = 0, LCR_s = 0, YR = YR)
maxdate = max(cbind(SPP$YDAY_1, SPP$YDAY_2, SPP$YDAY_3))
mindate = min(cbind(SPP$YDAY_1, SPP$YDAY_2, SPP$YDAY_3))
date_s = ????
det.p = predict(m.age2, type="det", newdata=newdat, appendData=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
I am much more conservative than Marc.  Unless one could justify (to others and not just to yourself) that the reason for missing data was not related to the factors being investigated, I would not plug in the averages or use fancier imputation methods.  If one can justify the use of the imputation methods, that's great.  But not at all just to make software not print errors or warnings.  This is especially true if one might face court challenges if some management decisions were to be based on your analysis.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Admittedly, I'm a bit cranky in my old age.

If this was for a Master's Thesis or a homework problem, the consequences of any action would likely not be major no matter what was done.  But hopefully one would be able to come to the conclusion that the data was "missing at random" and just toss those sites (because there are so few sites) or perform some simple imputation.

If this was for supporting an upcoming land management decision (or a medical decision for a pharmaceutical company), I would investigate and document the cause for the "missingness."  Depending on the kind of "missingness", I'd make a decision of whether to perform some sort of imputation, drop the offending sites, or not do the analysis at all and treat that as a lesson learned.  (Yes, I know few would feel they have the luxury of not doing the analysis.  But that might be considered more often than not.)  If the analysis is still to be performed and reported, then the missingness and the associated actions need to be well documented and justified and prominently included in the report.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm running the occuMulti models on five species. There's 330 sites. For each species, the number of locations with at least one detection ranges from 88 to 187.

I think I might be having a problem with predicting the marginal and conditional probabilities. For example, when I try to get the conditional probabilities for coyotes with fawns present across distance to forest edge, I use this code, based on what I've seen in the help file:

coyfp<-predict(m164,'state',species='coy',cond='fawn')

But when I plot the resulting predicted estimates using this code

plot(covraw$DISTED,coyfp$Predicted)

I get this graph:

So obviously I'm missing something in here. I've tried using code like this

coyfp<-predict(m164,'state',species='coy',cond=c('fawn','-hum','-bear','-bob')

And I get the same result, with perhaps the magnitude lower. I've also tried this for multiple species.

I'm not sure what's happening, I'm also having trouble with the conditional occupancy for a species when another species is absent not having any clear relationship to a covariate, despite having a clear one when the other species is present. I'm fully willing to believe I've made too complicated a model, but I just thought I'd ask.

Here's the model I'm working from

Thank you for any help!

Jennifer

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jim,

very thoughtful comments, thanks. These are big and important considerations and you are quite right to remind people of this big-picture perspective.

On the other hand, since Adrienne may not end up in a congress hearing with her study, I still think she could just choose the cheap solution and either mean-impute or drop. And since it’s such a minute part of her data set that’s missing, it won’t materially matter probably.

Best regards  - Marc

Von: unma...@googlegroups.com [mailto:unma...@googlegroups.com] Im Auftrag von Jim Baldwin
Gesendet: Dienstag, 11. Februar 2020 18:29
An: unma...@googlegroups.com
Betreff: Re: [unmarked] Error in parboot: invalid size argument

Admittedly, I'm a bit cranky in my old age.

If this was for a Master's Thesis or a homework problem, the consequences of any action would likely not be major no matter what was done.  But hopefully one would be able to come to the conclusion that the data was "missing at random" and just toss those sites (because there are so few sites) or perform some simple imputation.

If this was for supporting an upcoming land management decision (or a medical decision for a pharmaceutical company), I would investigate and document the cause for the "missingness."  Depending on the kind of "missingness", I'd make a decision of whether to perform some sort of imputation, drop the offending sites, or not do the analysis at all and treat that as a lesson learned.  (Yes, I know few would feel they have the luxury of not doing the analysis.  But that might be considered more often than not.)  If the analysis is still to be performed and reported, then the missingness and the associated actions need to be well documented and justified and prominently included in the report.

Jim

Thank you for the answer!! Ah, so if I understand this correctly, this is what I would use:

pcountOpen(~siteCov(s) ~siteCov(s) ~siteCov(s) ~obsCovs, data, ......), or as an option I could put 1's for "null".

I tried the function with some obscovs and sitecovs.

dm1 <- pcountOpen(~ 1 ~ 1 ~ 1 ~ 1, umf2, mixture = "NB", K = 120, dynamics = "constant", fix = "none", se = FALSE) #Null models
dm2 <- pcountOpen(~ 1 ~ 1 ~ 1 ~ Day, umf2, mixture = "NB", K = 120, dynamics = "constant", fix = "none", se = FALSE)
dm3 <- pcountOpen(~ 1 ~ 1 ~ Meadow ~ Day, umf2, mixture = "NB", K = 120, dynamics = "constant", fix = "none", se = FALSE)

However, in all cases, I get the following error:
Error in pcountOpen(~1 ~ 1 ~ Meadow ~ Day, umf2, mixture = "NB", K = 120,  : argument "omegaformula" is missing, with no default

Any idea?

Den mån 10 feb. 2020 kl 17:07 skrev John Clare <john....@maine.edu>:

> Hi Krisztina,
>
> Formulas in r (almost always or always incorporating the tilde in some fashion --e.g., y~x, y~1, etc.) are objects that help the fitting machinery find the necessary variables, set up the model matrix, and so forth. pcountOpen is no different in this regard: the first three arguments are formulas for models of initial abundance, recruitment, survival, etc., and so this is where one would specify a model for the variation in initial abundance/recruitment/survival with covariates and/or interactions/polynomials/other transformations. I think the only 'numbers' you need to provide unmarked are self contained in the unmarked frame (the detections in whatever form, distance bands for certain models, maybe something I'm forgetting). The formulas are looking for the same sort of compact description of the model structure regardless of the argument for 'dynamics', but maybe worth re-iterating the documentation in noting that the interpretation of the parameters changes depending upon how dynamics are specified.
>
> John

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am trying to test my best model using the GOF test with bootstrapping using the 'fitstats' and 'parboot' function, however, I keep running into an error.
My best model includes 5 covariates (continuous and categorical) for my state function (density), and 2 covariates for detection (continuous and categorical).
When I try to run the parboot function I get this error:

> (best.pb <- parboot(best, fitstats, nsim=10, report=5))
t0 = 161818.2 4068.05 3208.268
Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) :
  non-finite finite-difference value [18]

In playing around however, this error only seems to arise in 'parboot; when the "site" variable (categorical) is included in my detection part of the model. If I take this out, it runs. Why would this be?

In looking through other threads I've tried including different arguments in my model:
1. se = FALSE        --> I get the same error in parboot
2. method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = 0, upper = Inf       -->  When running the model in gdistsamp I get this error
In (new("standardGeneric", .Data = function (object)  :
  Model did not converge. Try providing starting values or increasing maxit control argment.
3. Include start values based on simpler model estimates (e.g. starts = c(-4, 0, 3))   --> this however causes the error: , and then R crashes. WIth any model, when
error:col::subvec (): did not converge. indices out of bounds or incorrectly used

I think the issue may my parameter estimates as the intercept estimate for abundance = -5.632 (see code for best model below). Which if I'm understanding it correctly, doesn't make sense since abundance can't be negative.
When I don't include covariates in my state model and leave as ~1, my abundance estimates are >0, only when I include covariates does the estimate go <1.
Does this make sense?

This is the output for my best model.
gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~site + roughness + closed.P + total.BA +
    shannon, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~site + closed.P, data = g.umf,
    keyfun = "halfnorm", output = "density", unitsOut = "kmsq",
    mixture = c("NB"), K = 150, se = TRUE)

Hi Bryan,

I would guess that the strange coefficient estimates for observer P reflects something strange about the data for observer P. Have you looked at the breakdown of the number of observations for each observer to see if there is anything unusual? Maybe P had a very small number of observations relative to the others or their actual observations had unusual values.

I would also try running the model without the data from that observer to see if runs without issues.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,
You might need to choose between using distance models and time removal models with unmarked (see gdistsamp, gmultmix functions). The R package 'detect' <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/detect/index.html> provides another option to model abundance and detection using both distance and time removal data (see cmulti function), but you may need to bootstrap for CIs, and I think the package provides a function to bootstrap.

There is an example of a time removal analysis using the gmultmix function in unmarked in the documentation (here <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/unmarked/versions/0.13-1/topics/gmultmix>).
Cheers,
Brian

Actually, I think I mis-spoke here: I think there should be another starting value corresponding to the decay parameter in the detection function ('sigma'...although I don't see it in the summary above?). Loosely speaking, the fitting procedure here is like an informed guess and check, and the starting values tell the optimizer where to start guessing.

> Perhaps I'm not inputting the starting values correctly though. For gistsamp the parameters are listed as (~lambda,~phi, ~p). So does this mean I should list all my estimates for abundance (17), then the estimate for phi, then the estimates for detection (14)?

...the simplest way to deal with this is something like starts =coef(model). Indices being out of bounds simply means that the number of starting values provided doesn't make sense: too few, too many, etc.

Yeah, don't do this. I haven't seen the original bit of advice advocating for setting upper and lower bounds, but doing this constrains every covariate to have some sort of positive effect. Moreover, because a lower bound of zero is imposed on the *link* scale, this puts some strange constraints on the intercepts for each parameter--for example, lambda has to be >= exp(0)  or >= 1 before any additive effects.

I think, assuming you were able to fit the model using 'BFGS', that this machinery should work okay for bootstrapping if provided reasonable start values. If it doesn't, there are potentially some deeper issues with the model fit.

John

> > > > > > > > > write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > #Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Must have same number of intervals, so use length.out instead of by interval
> > > > > > > > > NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20), ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,length.out=20))
> > > > > > > > > Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
> > > > > > > > > write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > #Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Mean of first covar and range of values for second
> > > > > > > > > NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=0, ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,by=0.1))
> > > > > > > > > Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
> > > > > > > > > write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > You can also use the min and max functions to population the sequence arguments in creating a data frame to predict into:
> > > > > > > > > Instead of RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20) use RRdist=seq(min(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),max(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),length.out=20)

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am running single season occupancy in Unmarked. I had model uncertainty and used the package "AICcmodavg" to get my conditional model averaged estimates (modavg() as opposed to modavgShrink()) given that I do not have equal representation of all of my covariates across models. That works fine and I have what my estimates should be. The issue that I am having now is that the modavgPred() function defaults to using modavgShrink() to get the estimates it uses for predictions. I have not found a way to change this and am wondering if anyone has had to do this in the past? Thinking that I could use another model averaging function in a different package I tried using the model.avg() function in the package MuMin. This averaged my estimates correctly, and I should be able to take the output and use it in the classic predict function. However the issue I am running into using MuMin has to do with overdispursion in my data (I have a c.hat of 1.86). The MuMin model.avg function correctly ranked models using QAICc, but is not inflating the standard errors by the square root of c.hat like it should. I tried the argument adjust.se <http://adjust.se> = TRUE as I saw someone reference online, but it does not work. Given this, my understanding is that I am unable to get correct confidence intervals on the predicted values. If anyone has dealt with this before I would appreciate any help! I have copied the functions in my code below. Thanks!

Kyle

avmodels <- list(o1,oG) ### Confidence set

avgm <- model.avg(avmodels,rank = "QAICc",rank.args = alist(chat = 1.86),
                  full = TRUE,revised.var = TRUE,
                  adjust=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Ty,

If the code works for one species, but not the other, it might be that some models cannot estimate the parameter you are interested in. Are the model lists for both species identical? A first place to start would be to do a quick check with the function extractX(your.model.list) to see if the output is identical. Also, you might want to consider model-averaging with shrinkage instead (modavgShrink( )), especially if you have a lot of uncertainty regarding the top models, or looking at the model-averaged predictions (modavgPred( )) as a function of different values of your explanatory variable.

Best,

Marc

messages.body_plain:
Kyle,

Model-averaging predictions should be based on the entire set of models and is the "original" way to do multimodel inference à la Burnham and Anderson (2002). I don't see why you would want to average predictions just on certain models.

That being said, if you really want to do average based on certain models, then you could use modavgCustom( ) which averages predictions or betas, based on the values of log-likelihood, number of estimated parameters, estimates, and SE's (?modavgCustom). This would get you what you want, but see my comment above.

Marc

If you want to get predictions that account for the support of each model in your set, then you should do predictions using each model and model-average these values to get your model-averaged predictions. This is what you get with modavgPred( ) and this is the usual way model-averaging predictions works.

Good luck,

Marc

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Error message using modavg function (AICcmodavg package) - Parameter not found
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ty,

The difference between both is that modavg( ) computes the "natural
average" of the estimate (Burnham and Anderson 2002, p. 152). If you
have several models that share the support, then this estimate could be
biased high (Cade 2015: Ecology 96, 2370--2382), because it only
focuses on the models that include the parameter of interest. In such a
case, model-averaging with the shrinkage estimator is preferred
(Burnham and Anderson 2002, p. 152) as it includes all models (e.g.,
modavgShrink( )).

Regarding your issues with the two species, you can send me offlist
your code and data so I can take a look.

Hope it helps,

Marc

messages.subject: Building a loop to calculate cumulative estimates from camtrapR detection histories
messages.subject_clean: Building a loop to calculate cumulative estimates from camtrapR detection histories
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I have a number of detection histories produced in camtrapR from camera trapping data and am interested in calculating cumulative detection probability from occasion 1 to occasion n. I know I can do this in a long-winded way by truncating each detection history to 1 occasion, then 2 occasions, 3 occasions, etc., but this will take a considerable amount of time with 9 detection histories and 50-60 occasions in most of those, and increases the risk of simply misplacing information with all the data frames that will be produced

I'm hoping that there might be a way to set up a loop so that I can automate this process to fill in a blank matrix, preferably with p and upper and lower 95% confidence intervals (i.e. a 3-row matrix, with varying columns depending on the detection history used). I have no real experience working with loops, but perhaps somebody here has experience doing just that and might be able to help out. I think a for loop is the way I need to go about doing this, but I don't know how I would set up the loop to iterate cumulative occasions from 1 to n. Any ideas?

Thanks,
Jarrad

messages.subject_clean: Building a loop to calculate cumulative estimates from camtrapR detection histories
messages.body_plain:
For those interested, I think this is the way to do it, at least to get detection probabilities quickly calculated to show how it changes over time. I imagine it's reasonably straightforward to work out cumulative detection probability from the resulting matrix:

Dets <- dat[,-1] #produce detection history without "station" col

pmat <- matrix(nrow = 1, ncol = 58) #produce empty matrix of 1 row and cols = ncol(Dets)

for(i in seq_along(pmat)) {
m1 <- occu(~1 ~1, data = unmarkedFrameOccu(y = Dets[1:i]))
m1.psi <- backTransform(m1, type = "state")
m1.p <- backTransform(m1, type = "det")
pmat[i] = m1.p@estimate
}

messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of OccuMulti output
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’m very sorry for this basic question but I need some help interpreting the output of the occuMulti function. I am trying to model the occupancy of two species (puma and collared peccary) in the presence of some detection variables and occupancy variables.

I built the frame like this:

puma_peccary<-unmarkedFrameOccuMulti(y=list(pumaoccupancy, peccaryoccupancy), siteCovs=var.site, obsCovs = var.obs)

So far so good. I made a “null” model assuming constant detection and constant occupancy for both species like this:

m0<-occuMulti(c('~1','~1'), c('~1','~1','~1'), puma_peccary)

The output of this model looks like this:

Occupancy:

                      Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)

[sp1] (Intercept)       0.0794 0.595  0.133   0.894

[sp2] (Intercept)      -0.2794 0.661 -0.423   0.672

[sp1:sp2] (Intercept)   1.1282 0.866  1.303   0.193

Detection:

                  Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

[sp1] (Intercept)   -0.842 0.160 -5.26 1.41e-07

[sp2] (Intercept)   -1.169 0.193 -6.07 1.32e-09

AIC: 599.9831

>From this output, I’m guessing sp1 is puma and sp2 is collared peccary. Is it correct to conclude from this output that there is a positive correlation between the occupancy of puma and peccary (estimate 1.1282). I understand this relation is not significant, I’m just trying to understand what the output tells me.

I am working on a set of candidate models that are designed to test the effects of certain detection variables and certain occupancy variables, but if it’s possible I would like to add presence/absence of a certain species to these terms as well. For example: does presence of puma have an influence on peccary detection? Is there any way I can include this?

Thanks for the help!
